utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Mr. Huber for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, may we have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I am Edina Residovic, counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Together with me is here, Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada. Your Honours, I believe that there was a confusion yesterday. The witnesses who we called were on the list of witnesses. I would like to draw your attention to the fact that this list is dated 20th of May and they were indicated as Witnesses B and C on that list. These witnesses are actually witness Delalic and witness Ciso and I apologise if we had caused this confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Today I am sitting in for my colleagues Mr. Olujic and Mr. Tomislav Kuzmanovic who are away from the seat of the Tribunal for professional reasons. On behalf of Mr. Zdravko Mucic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my name is Salih Karabdic, I am an attorney from Sarajevo and I defend Mr. Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I am Cynthia McMurrey, along with my colleague, Ms. Nancy Boler. We represent Mr. Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much, Ms. Residovic, for your correction. But actually the Trial Chamber was relying on the latest lists of witnesses, so I am happy for your correction. Please invite the witness. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Remind the witness he's still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may. ISMET CISO

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ciso, I hope you've had some rest and I hope that you feel a bit better this morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I feel a lot better, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I told you to wait for the interpretation of my question and I would kindly ask you to do so today, again, so that the interpreters do not have to interrupt us and draw our attention to that fact. Mr. Ciso, yesterday you indicated that you, Dzemal Delalic and Elvir, assisted by a young woman, a refugee from Bosnia-Herzegovina that you had put up a so-called, an unedited tape, do you remember saying that before the Tribunal yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you did with these raw copies of the videotape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These two or three unedited tapes were taken by myself and Sefik to Zagreb and we handed them over to the journalist, Ekrem Milic. And Sefik took that opportunity because he, himself, had taken part in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so he took this opportunity to clarify a number of things that were quite significant for journalist, Milic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ekrem Milic, did he believe at that time that he had enough material and what was his idea as to how you should proceed with the tape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ekrem Milic told us that he would have a look at these raw copies. That it was easier for him to work with two or three tapes instead of twenty or even thirty tapes, so he took these tapes with him and he told us that he would inform us later on, through Vaso, what he had done with the tapes. And he also indicated that he would make, he would compose a text to go with these video recordings. And we were supposed to edit the texts, together with the tape in Vienna later on. And put up a final version of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciso, what was the purpose of that tape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, that tape was supposed to be some kind of denial to the negative articles that had appeared in Croatian press about the Town of Konjic, about Mr. Zejnil Delalic himself and about the general situation in the area. It was supposed to be some kind of counter campaign to these negative texts of the media in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your involvement with that tape, was it completed with that conversation in Zagreb or were you in any way involved again in the edition of this tape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My involvement did not stop at that point, but our work in Vienna had almost been completed. We were waiting for a report and for professional editing of that tape from Mr. Ekrem Milic, which happened very soon after that. And Dzemal told me, maybe after 10 days, Ekrem sent the tapes back, together with his comments on them, comments that were supposed to go with the video recordings and with the text that we were supposed to insert in the final version of the tape. He wrote us as to how we should proceed with the editing of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you follow the instructions that you had received from Mr. Milic and who did that and where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We fully complied with the instruction given to us by Mr. Milic and we trusted him. We trusted that it had been done in a professional way because this is a journalist task. So as soon as we received the materials, we went to the premises of Inda-Bau company, where we had all the necessary technical equipment available to edit the final version of the tape. And Dzemal, Elvir and myself and this young woman that I mentioned and whom we had asked to read the text, we started putting up the final version of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciso, can you remember today the text that you inserted in the videotape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well that tape was not such an important subject in my life. I know it has become important in these proceedings, but it's very difficult for me to remember all the details. However, there are certain things that I do remember. The most significant parts, the most significant segments of the texts, for example, which to me as a lay person sounded a bit pompous. Let me give you an example. For example, Mr. Delalic, he was accused of being a Serb spy and he had fled in a Chetnik helicopter and so on. Those had been the allegations and Ekrem Milic, in order to counter such a propaganda, wrote that he had detained Serbs in prisons in that area. So I, again, as I say, it seemed, for me it was difficult to accept because I am a lay person, I don't know anything about that. But I cannot tell you more about the details in connection with this tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciso, could you remember what was suggested as the ending of the tape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would rather start with the beginning of the tape. You must remember that this was also the beginning of the creation of our state and Ekrem, as a person who knew about editing, told us that we should insert a scene with the flag of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that this should be the beginning of the tape. And the end, he said should be Zejnil's first arrival from Bosnia-Herzegovina and the meeting in Inda-Bau company because it was a very emotional event. So he thought that this should be a suitable moment for the ending of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to this suggestion, as to how to finish the tape, did you also follow the instructions of Mr. Milic, or did you add something yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't add anything. I didn't make any proposals in connection with the tape because I believe that it had been done in a professional way. However Dzemal Delalic had a video recording of a very brief statement made by Mr. Zejnil Delalic, which had been given to him by Zejnil. And which he thought, which he wanted, as he had told me, which he wanted to send to Sarajevo in order to express his dissatisfaction with the general situation in the area at that moment. So Dzemal said that this should, perhaps, be the best ending of the final version of the tape, which we did, which we accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciso, did Dzemal tell you when Zejnil Delalic had recorded that statement? The one that was suggested by Dzemal as the ending of the tape.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't ask him about that and I don't know when that video recording was made, but I assume that it was done after his arrival in Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After you had edited the tape, according to Milic's instructions and after you had inserted that portion suggested by Dzemal, what did you do with the tape afterwards? If you can tell us that. If yourself took part in it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did take part in the editing of the tape. We took it back to Ekrem Milic in Zagreb. We wanted him to see the tape and to give his assessment of the quality of our work. We wanted to know whether we had managed to follow his instructions in making up the tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any objections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A few days later Ekrem was in touch with us and he said that we had put significant effort in editing the tape. However, he thought that the final product was an amateur tape and that he didn't quite appreciate the way the text was read. He thought that this should have been done by a professional, a radio reporter, for example. And he thought that the tape could fulfil its purpose, but he said that he didn't want to do that without the approval of Zejnil Delalic himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself ask Zejnil's approval? That is, did you ever show him the tape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. When Ekrem Milic returned the tape to us, he had sent it by coach from Zagreb. Dzemal and his wife Suada took the tape and went to Munich to see Zejnil. I would have probably gone myself if I had had a visa, but it was very difficult for us to go to Germany from Austria, in spite of the fact that I was employed in Austria. Anyway, Suada and Dzemal took the tape to Zejnil in Munich and they wanted him to review the tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what Zejnil thought about the tape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the same day, in the evening, Zejnil called my apartment and he told me that he was really moved by our attention and by our attempts to fight the media. However, he expressed his opinion as to the tape itself and thought that the tape did not really correspond; did not meet standards, technical standards, and was not true in terms of comments. He thought there were lots of exaggerations in the description of the events and so on. He said that he did not want the tape to reach the public; however, he said that he would try and use some other methods to defend his respect and his integrity. He was thinking of hiring lawyers and taking some kind of legal action.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you accept such a position of Mr. Zejnil Delalic and was it at the end of your involvement with the tape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this is something that you had to accept because it was a personal thing of Mr. Zejnil Delalic. I mean, we would have been liars again if we had released such a tape without his approval. So of course we heeded his advice, and that's how we proceeded, that is, the tape remained as a souvenir to a couple of us who were working on it, and this is something that I have at home in my private videotapes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ciso, after your involvement with the tape, did you later on, at any point in time, meet with Mr. Zejnil Delalic and when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After our last meeting in the premises of Inda-Bau in Vienna, I met with Zejnil Delalic. I cannot tell you the exact date, but I know that it was after the funeral of his brother Sefik in Vienna. It was his personal tragedy. He lost two brothers on the same day, Sefik in Vienna and Vejsil in Zagreb. They both died of natural causes within the time frame of two hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you, Mr. Ciso, present at these funerals and was Mr. Delalic also present at these funerals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was present at the funerals. The first one was held in Zagreb when Vejsil was being buried. We from Konjic, friends of the family, acquaintances, attended. We went to Zagreb, but Zejnil didn't go to the funeral in Zagreb because that was the time of the fiercest conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council, so that he stayed behind in Vienna and we attended the funeral which was fully secured by members of the military police of the HVO and by the Croatian police as well. Probably Mr. Zejnil Delalic's arrival was expected and he would have probably been arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Ciso, since you met him at his brother's funeral at Vienna, so this is the other funeral that Zejnil Delalic did attend in Vienna; did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At the funeral in Vienna, Zejnil Delalic was present, and that was the first time I saw him after our last meeting in Inda-Bau when he had returned from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciso, did you cooperate with Mr. Delalic later on and did you come across one another in Vienna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would meet with Mr. Zejnil Delalic in Vienna, and our contacts were particularly close when a new society of Bosnia-Herzegovina was being established, a society of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Austria, which was inaugurated in the summer or the beginning of the autumn of 1993 in the Taubergasse Street number 15 in the 17th Vienna district.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any position in that club?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. From the very foundation of the club, which numbered 400 to 500 members, I was a member of the main board from the very outset, the Vice-President of the BH society and president of the executive board of the BH society in Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What were the activities of that club?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me emphasise that we are an Austrian society registered in the Republic of Austria as our host country. The aim of the society upon its registration was humanitarian, sports, cultural and other activities of citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Austria, regardless of religion, as well as of Austrian citizens who were sympathisers and members of this BH society.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Mr. Ciso, whether any events from Bosnia-Herzegovina were reviewed and discussed and was relief collected for Bosnia-Herzegovina in that club?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the BH society became one of the most powerful societies in Austria and even in Europe. We organised various cultural events like art exhibitions, evenings of films. We organised demonstrations when any current developments in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina required it. The events in Srebrenica and so on, all this with the approval of the Austrian authorities. We were privileged to have distinguished visitors attend our events, that is, citizens of Austria such as, for instance, Mr. Simon Wiesenthal at an art exhibition. In the area of sports, we formed a football league and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think that is sufficient for us to have an idea of the activities of the club. Tell us, Mr. Ciso, was Zejnil Delalic a member of the club and of the main board?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Zejnil Delalic was a member of the club. He was a member of the main board, and I think that he headed the department for relations with other societies and organisations in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- no, in Europe.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you organised fund-raising. Did you send those funds to Jablanica and Konjic and other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What we cared about most was that the relief should reach Bosnia-Herzegovina. We did collect funds and the media in Bosnia-Herzegovina reported about our activities. We bought hospital beds, wheelchairs, assistance for the nurseries and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, personally, sometimes carry that relief to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had the pleasure and satisfaction immediately after the conflict between the BiH army and the HVO to drive relief to the Electro Konjic in Konjic. This company had very serious problems. They could not provide electricity for hospitals and maternity wards. I don't remember whether it was October or November, but I drove a truck full of humanitarian aid that I presented to the electricity supply board in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I just read in the transcript that this was immediately after the conflict between the army and the HVO. Is that a mistake in the translation or is that what you said, after the end of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after the end of the conflict, otherwise we couldn't have reached them at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did your society have videotapes and did they lend them out for other members of the group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did all kinds of things. We had certain media significance. The whole of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina knew about us, and it was a society for all citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina wherever they came from, so that many came to visit us, people engaged in logistics, representatives of the authorities, refugees, people who were there and who had managed to escape, so that we received quite a number of such tapes which we would show in our premises. Hosts of people would come to view their country, the suffering of their people, their relatives, the members of their family, friends, so that with the assistance of our sponsors, we managed to copy those tapes and even to send them on to societies in Linz, Salzburg --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me whether the Inda-Bau company was one of your sponsors for this kind of activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Inda-Bau company was one of the sponsors of the BH society from its very establishment. Then there's the company Septor (phoen), many construction companies. Inda-Bau was our sponsor when it came to technical facilities, the copying of tapes, copying of various kinds, because this was of great assistance to us. They provided all kinds of crucial support for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Ciso, did a part of those tapes and some of your own documents; were they sometimes placed in the premises of the Inda-Bau, either permanently or temporarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Inda-Bau was, in a sense, a kind of forward outpost or a depot. With the arrest of Mr. Zejnil Delalic by The Hague Tribunal, we learned after that that a certain quantity, a certain number of our tapes had disappeared, as well as other documentation. We reacted immediately to this by addressing the Inda-Bau company and asking for an explanation for the disappearance of this material which we considered to be of vital importance for our future work. You yourself, Ms. Edina Residovic, as Defence counsel of Mr. Zejnil Delalic, was addressed by us, but to this day, we haven't regained possession of the materials and the tapes, and you have explained to us that you were not in a position to assist us in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciso, yesterday during your testimony, you said that you were in Konjic twice in the course of 1992 and later on, probably in '94, after the end of the conflict that you referred to today. In 1992 when you visited Konjic, did you visit the Celebici barracks on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never visited the Celebici barracks. Believe me, I never had even time to think about it and it was in no way of any interest to me, nor did I visit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciso, thank you. Your Honours, that ends my examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ciso. My name is Nico Duric, and I'm appearing today on behalf of Mr. Zdravko Mucic known as "Pavo." Tell me please, do you know Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Mr. Mucic as a co-citizen of mine and a colleague from work, during a certain period of time in Austria.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know his family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I know his son Zoran, his daughter Sandra and his ex-wife Alisa.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in September 1992, did you see Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean in Austria? It was most refreshing for me to come across Mr. Zdravko Mucic when he came to Austria because he brought me greetings from my family, my ill parents. During that stay, he was my guest in my home and he spent the night in my apartment. This was in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know how much time he spent in Vienna at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite a bit because he wouldn't let me sleep at night. We would stay awake talking but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the court what did you do for Mr. Mucic at the time? Did you look for an apartment for him or something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Mucic told me that his children were not cared for, that he was looking for an apartment for them, that he would like to enrol them at school, because he already had the status of a temporarily employed worker in Austria. So I think that during that visit, he managed to find an apartment for his children in the 16th or 17th district.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you do the official registration for him in Vienna at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I can't really remember whether it was myself or my son, but he wasn't very lucky on that occasion too because the police said his tires were not in good shape, so he paid a heavy fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Ciso, on the 27th of July, what does that date represent in the former Yugoslavia? What did it represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the insurrection day of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the former Yugoslavia. I think so. I'm not a very good historian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that in those days it was a rather important holiday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sufficiently important to be declared an official state holiday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Pavo, was he with you on that day in 1992 and where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am unable to remember. Perhaps you could refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Was he with you in Vienna on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did stay with me in Vienna but I couldn't remember exactly the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: But you could confirm that he was in Vienna at the end of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. More or less every time he came, he would call and we would spend time together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we agree, the two of us, whether Pavo, in 1992, spent more time in Vienna than in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, he made quite a number of trips, probably on account of his children, to provide for them, to enrol them at school. I think he came to Vienna several times, I can't remember exactly. But he would always be helpful because I would send food and medicines to my parents through him to Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: But that was very frequently in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite frequently, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Would you tell me, please, whether Pavo was a good friend of Mr. Sefik Delalic's?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How good a friend he was, I don't know, but I know that they knew one another and that they would get together occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ciso.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any other cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: The Defence of Hazim Delic has no questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The Defence of Esad Landzo has no questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Cross-examination by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: My name is Theresa McHenry, and on behalf of the Prosecution I'm going to ask you a few questions. I ask that you listen carefully to my question, and if you don't understand it, please tell me. Also, when you can, please answer the question with just a "yes" or "no" or "I don't know." Now, Mr. Ciso, what kind of work do you do in Vienna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vienna, I had several jobs. My first job was on a construction site. My second one was washing dishes in a hospital. My third was in a warehouse. My fourth, I did all kinds of work in Austria.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Have you ever done any type of journalism work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have never practised any journalism, but I was head of the section for information in the BH society in Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, you clearly have a close relationship with the Delalic family. Is your relationship purely personal or do you have any business interest with any members of the Delalic family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have friendly relations with the Delalic family. First of all, we come from the same area. Then there were some joint business contacts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when was this video made, the video that you've spoken about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was made, I can't exactly remember the details, but roughly from mid January until the end of March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you estimate, just roughly, about how many hours you spent on this project including editing, travel, meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you how many hours because I didn't keep any record of that activity, nor on other activities that I engaged in for Bosnia-Herzegovina and various humanitarian efforts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, the young man from Inda-Bau who assisted Elvir, what's his full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The young man from Inda-Bau who assisted Elvir? I don't understand your question. It may have been Elvir from Inda-Bau who assisted us. There is no third person. I think you're probably thinking of Elvir, a young man from Inda-Bau who helped us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm not sure I understand the name. If I may mix it up again, so, if so, please correct me. The person from Inda-Bau who helped you, what is his full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His name is Elvir Rizvanovic and he is a native of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was he in Konjic during the war at all, during 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was not. I think not. I couldn't tell you for sure. I couldn't really give you an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The woman from the association who helped you, what is her name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Her name is Harisa Prevljak, and later she was the girlfriend of Elvir and later she became his wife, so her name changed to Rizvanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was she in Konjic in 1992, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't say, but I do know that we would see one another before the war. And at the very beginning of the war when refugees started coming, I think that was when she came to Vienna too, but I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is she from Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So besides you, Mr. Rizvanovic, his wife, the journalist, Mr. Milic, and Vejsil and Dzemal Delalic, did anyone else work on the project?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sefik, the brother, the late brother of Zejnil Delalic, was working on this project with me who went to Zagreb with me once or twice carrying those tapes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: During all the work you did on this project, including travelling to Zagreb on several occasions, did you pay for those expenses yourself or were they reimbursed in some way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whatever I did for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its citizens, refugees, and considering this too to be my duty as a citizen of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the first place, and also as a native of Konjic, I did all this at my own expense and that is why at the end of this war I have very high credit rates to pay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Mr. Milic, the journalist, did he receive any kind of remuneration for his efforts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Milic, a journalist, I really cannot answer that question. These are personal matters and I think you should better ask him. I didn't pay him, nor did he receive any compensation from me. As for the rest, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milic, you stated he was from Bosnia. Was he from Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Milic, Ekrem, is not from Konjic. He is from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think that he originally came from Foca or Eastern Bosnia but I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If you know, was Mr. Milic in Konjic, during 1992, during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that he told me about going to Sarajevo, saying that he was a refugee in Croatia. Whether he was in Konjic or not, I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: May I interrupt for just a brief moment? On the transcript, we keep getting the wrong spelling of the last name of this Mr. Milic. It's M-I-L-I-C, not M-E-L-I-C. It should be changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you were in Bosnia in 1992, were you involved at all in any military activities or did you just bring and deliver things for your family members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My main task, at the time, was to take care of my family and my friends, and I never took any part in fighting or any military operations, and I never spent longer than two or three days in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina during my visits at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated that Dzemal Delalic was in Bosnia in 1992 and was involved in certain activities there. Can you just give us an idea, to the extent you know, of what kind of activities he was involved in? I'm asking things like, was he a soldier; what was his position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean Dzemal Delalic?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Dzemal, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know much about his involvement in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. All I know is that whenever he went there, he would always be carrying humanitarian aid that we had collected through various organisations. As for his specific involvement in Bosnia and Herzegovina during the war, I couldn't tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly to indicate that Dzemal mostly lived in Vienna and, like you, would just travel back to Bosnia for short visits?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And how about, and please forgive me if I pronounce it wrong, Mr. Vejsil Delalic? Was he in Konjic at the time of the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't give you an answer to that question, I don't know. He was our liaison person in Zagreb, whether he went to Konjic or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: But as far as you know, in 1992, he was basically living in Zagreb, though he may have travelled to Konjic on occasion? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that he was living in Zagreb at the time, whether he went to Konjic and to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And how about Mr. Sefik Delalic, was he living in Konjic during the war of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sefik Delalic had a status of a temporarily employed worker in Austria even before the war. And during the war, he would go to Konjic from time to time, though his family lived in Vienna, his wife and his child. He, therefore, worked there, but he would occasionally travel to Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, sir, you indicated that Mr. Delalic was the victim of a propaganda campaign after he returned to Vienna and that he was, among other things, accused of helping Serbs. My question is, sir, did you know it was reported by others and acknowledged by Mr. Delalic that he was also being accused in the Serb media of being a war criminal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question, if it's not asking too much?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Certainly, sir. You indicated that when Mr. Delalic returned, he was the victim of a propaganda campaign and you talked about some reports in Croatian papers. I am asking if you are aware that there were reports in the Serb media where Mr. Delalic was being charged with being a war criminal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't know, I mean I cannot give you an answer to your question. At that time I didn't have access to the Serb media.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you talk about Mr. Delalic and various members were being charged with various things, were you aware that among the things that Mr. Delalic was being investigated or charged with in the media were both allegations of murder and certain events related to the Celebici camp? Were you aware of those reports? And I am speaking about the time that you were involved in this video project.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I have never heard such a piece of information in my life and I have never heard a thing like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated that even though no one believed the propaganda against Mr. Delalic, you thought that these stories somehow constituted a threat to Mr. Delalic and his family. Were these stories more of a threat than existed, when Mr. Delalic had a significant and a public commanding role in the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that these reports would not have been made on that basis. It is a fact that Zejnil had invested a lot of his knowledge, his efforts, his money in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and I think that that was the basic motive. As for his commanding responsibility and role, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am not sure if I made my question clear. My question was specifically whether or not, during the time that Mr. Delalic was actually involved in the war, when he was in Konjic and other areas in 1992, as I understand you, there was no particular threat to him or to his family then, but you believed there was one later because of the negative newspaper articles? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated that Mr. Zejnil Delalic had a number of tapes, twenty to thirty, whose tapes were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These videotapes belonged to everyone. Dzemal kept bringing in some tapes, Sefik, myself and we used the material from the Konjic TV as well. It has its regular broadcast at that time, Sarajevo TV, Hadzic TV. And some of the materials were recorded on a private basis, so I cannot specify who the owner of the tapes was. Each of us had a number of tapes and we gave them -- we wanted them to be used to make this one final videotape.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, if any of these tapes were Mr. Zejnil Delalic's tapes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know if any of these tapes belonged to him. I couldn't tell you anything about that. It was not such an important thing for me, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's fine. There's nothing wrong to say you don't know when you don't know. You don't have to explain why. Were these tapes labelled or organised or did they have their own narration explaining what was going on. Can you just tell me a little bit about how they were organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, every tape had a title, more or less, so that the owner could remember that it was his tape and so that we can remember the contents of the video. We would use stickers, so I believed that each of the tapes had a label on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And do you remember, did any of the tapes have narration on them? For instance, if they were of a battle, somebody is in the background telling you where the battle is taking place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these voices belonged to various radio reporters. I don't know, I am not quite sure I understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, what happened to those tapes? Do you know where they are now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A number of tapes remained with the BH Society. And then certain tapes were at the Inda-Bau company and some of the tapes are in the possession of all of us. I mean, they are part of our private collection. But most of them remained at the Inda-Bau company because that is where we made the editing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were there any tapes of Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember any tape that would show something more than it was shown by the official TV. And here I am referring to the official Konjic TV. I haven't seen any tape that would provide more information about the Celebici facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, if I understood you correctly, and please correct me if I am wrong. That, in fact, the actual editing of the videotape was in the recording of the audio portion of the video was done by you in Inda-Bau with the equipment in Inda-Bau, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The editing was made by Elvir, Dzemal, myself and Harisa, who was the announcer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, was it correct that the editing and the recording was all done by using Inda-Bau's microphones, video equipment, cutting equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And what kind of business is Inda-Bau?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Inda-Bau is a construction company, which was involved with all kinds of construction works.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, with respect to the editing job that you and the others did at Inda-Bau, you must have done a good job because -- well, let me just ask you. Is the video footage that you prepared, and when I say "you", I mean the group at Inda-Bau, sir, that the group of you prepared, that's the same as the copy that was returned for Mr. Milic after he had looked at it, correct? Let me ask my question, maybe in a more clear way. Is it correct that Mr. Milic did not make any additional edits to the video that you provided him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we edited the tape and Mr. Milic directed it and he composed the text that was supposed to be inserted together with the editing. And we did all the technical part of the work.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now you indicated that after you had edited the tape, you and Mr. Dzemal Delalic went to Zagreb and met with the journalist and Mr. Dzemal Delalic gave him certain information about the tape, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you haven't understood me correctly. I said that we took two or three tapes to Zagreb, that is is Sefik and myself, and that we gave them to Mr. Ekrem Milic. And I also said that Sefik had made certain details clear in connection with the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And when you took two or three tapes to Zagreb, were those two or three copies of the same tape or were the two or three tapes different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were different. There were summaries. And I am talking about raw cuts of maybe twenty or thirty tapes. And we carefully edited with a lot of cutting work, so as to make a final version. Therefore, it was the summary of a number of twenty or thirty tapes and maybe two or three tapes. And this is what we believed to be the most important part.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And during the meeting you and Mr. Sefik and Mr. Milic had, about how long did that meeting last, where Mr. Sefik Delalic told Mr. Milic certain information about the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Present there was also Vejsil and we spent maybe two or three hours together.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you and the others decided to help Mr. Zejnil Delalic by making this video. Now, you would agree with me that another way to counter this negative propaganda would have been to say that Mr. Delalic had no influence or power whatsoever, that there was no way he could not have done these things, was that possibility considered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were sure and convinced that Zejnil Delalic was nobody's spy. That he was a fighter of the BiH army and we were sure that he hadn't committed any crimes and that he was not a war profiteer. And we were convinced that he was an honourable and respected citizen of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. My question was, did you and the others consider, as a way of countering this propaganda, that you could just simply state that Mr. Delalic had no position or power in Konjic and, thus, could not have done the things that he was accused of? Was that possibility considered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did consider the possibility to show certain denials, which would be stronger than the allegations that were being put forward. I don't know how else to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me just turn to something else then, maybe we can come back to that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Or see the alternative?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, he doesn't tell me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He doesn't have to tell you an alternative which he did not choose.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If he didn't consider it or if they didn't discuss it, that was all I was asking.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you're aware that during this time that you were involved in making this video, Mr. Delalic was himself involved in countering the negative publicity against him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of that. At that time, he didn't undertake anything. He was weathering a very difficult crisis, emotional and mental crisis. At that time I didn't notice any particular activities that he was undertaking. And I think that what we did was also the result of the state that he was in.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, were you aware that at some point, Mr. Delalic became involved in countering the stories against him? And that, for instance, he and others on his behalf wrote letters to newspapers and things like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you made this video, who did you plan on sending the video to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After we had finished, we had done the final version, we sent it to the requesting person, that is Mr. Milic. And Milic intended, provided that Zejnil agrees after he's reviewed the tape, he intended to organise a press conference to distribute the videotape to various newspapers and TV stations in case we would reach an agreement. That was the intention.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And why was it that, rather than getting Mr. Delalic's permission in the beginning of this project before everyone had put in this work, why was it waited until the project was almost completed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when a man finds himself in a difficult psychological situation, we wanted to surprise him pleasantly with that work. And we believed that he would agree to our sending this tape, to releasing the tape into the public. However, this didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you stated when you and Mr. Dzemal Delalic first talked with the journalist, Mr. Milic, the purpose was to -- Mr. Milic, "agreed to help uncover the truth"? I am quoting from what you said yesterday. Was the plan for this video to uncover the truth or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The intention was not to uncover the truth because Ekrem Milic was not in a position to uncover the truth. He was simply working on the basis of the material that we brought him. He didn't have any material or any tapes. He only had information that he had heard from the media. He was simply a professional journalist who was supposed to put the final touch on our work.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was the work supposed to, at the time that you were working on this project, was the work supposed to be truthful or untruthful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At any rate, the contents were supposed to be of a documentary nature. And it and was supposed to be truthful. However, Milic thought that this should be somehow exaggerated. I don't know how to explain myself, I am not an expert for journalism. But this too was supposed to be somehow modified so that it can serve that purpose. The events were supposed to be exaggerated and more -- they were suppose to require more significance than they really had.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, at the time that you were working on this project, do I understand you, you were aware that the project was supposed to modify the truth to serve Mr. Delalic's purposes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, couldn't you put it this way: The purpose was to deny the falsehood which did allege?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, I think I am certainly entitled to ask this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So am I entitled to understand what the witness was saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What he says is that the tape was intended to as a rebuttal to the falsehood that was being spread, so they exaggerated the role of Mr. Zejnil Delalic. So to put it in a --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is it correct that in an effort to help Mr. Delalic and to rebut the charges that you thought were false, you were part of this project which was not going to be a full description of the truth? Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He hadn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he's said he's modified the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have to tell something to uncover the truth. I think he's probably said that you have to tell a lie to counter a lie.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is that correct, sir, that this videotape was supposed to be a lie to counter what you believe were lies against him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The honourable judge gave a precise definition to what I was trying to explain. This tape simply was supposed to blow up the importance of Zejnil Delalic in that area at the time, so as to counter the lies that were being spread.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So, do I understand you, that it was supposed to be close to the truth so that it would be believed, but it wasn't exactly the truth so it would help Mr. Delalic. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The videotape was true, however, the comments blew up the importance and the role of Mr. Delalic at the time. I think that this would be more or less my answer to your questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, let me just make sure I understand. When you say "blow up the importance", do you mean that the information was not correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He's answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If Your Honour is directing me to go on, I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Nobody is prodding you to go forward. But when the questions you ask have been answered correctly, I think, it would not be fair for you to press such questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated that you knew Mr. Mucic rather well, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all residents of Konjic know each other, it's not a big town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: (Microphone not on).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am just asking him to clarify that before my next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, did Mr. Mucic ever show you any of his videotapes taken from Konjic, during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Are you aware if whether or not at any time Mr. Mucic made his own efforts to counter the propaganda campaign against Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of any other efforts, besides the video project you were involved in, are you aware of any other efforts made to counter the negative publicity where Mr. Delalic's role was blown up or exaggerated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am asking you whether or not, even if you yourself weren't involved in them, are you aware of any other efforts made by anyone to counter the negative publicity against Mr. Delalic where, as part of the effort, the role of Mr. Delalic was exaggerated or blown up? And if you don't know, you can just say I don't know of any.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it's right for us to break and reassemble at noon. The Trial Chamber will now rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. McHenry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I gathered from your testimony that you're aware that a videotape called "The War in Bosnia-Herzegovina," the videotape that you were involved in preparing, was seized, was taken. Do you know whose copy it was that was seized by the Austrian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That copy of the video, I think, that was seized -- the copy that was seized, I think, belonged to the BH society, I think. I'm not quite sure. It wasn't my own private copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So you had your own private copy and the Bosnian society had their own copy, is that correct, or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do know, yes. I had a copy and so did the BH society. For me, it is a souvenir, a momento.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And who provided the copy to the Bosnian society?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are members of that BH society, so all the people working on the tape were members of the BH society.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Delalic did not have any connection with the Inda-Bau premises in Vienna, did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that he would visit occasionally with his brother Dzemal. What connection he had, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, he certainly didn't keep any papers, documents or videos there, did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The BH society would leave some of its materials in the Inda-Bau company because our space was limited and this was a safe place to keep this material in. So in addition to videotapes, we kept some other documents that belonged to the Bosnia-Herzegovina society there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think maybe my question wasn't understood. Mr. Zejnil Delalic did not keep any videos or papers in the Vienna premises of Inda-Bau, did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm unable to answer that question. I think you should ask people working in Inda-Bau and people who were in charge of that company, so I don't have any knowledge about such things.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated that Mr. Delalic did not support the publication of this video because it was not entirely accurate. Sir, if there are any documents written or signed by Mr. Delalic about his role, you have no information to suggest that what is reported in those documents is blown up or exaggerated, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic explicitly and emphatically said "No, this is not a means of struggle that I want to use. I will use other means by engaging a lawyer and the like."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, my question is: If there are documents that were written or signed by Mr. Zejnil Delalic, you have no information to suggest that what is in those documents is in any way blown up or exaggerated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: First ask him whether he has seen those documents. It's only then he can say whether the accounts therein were exaggerated or not. Ask him if he has seen those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he has no information -- he may information even if he didn't actually see it. If he has no information whatsoever, I assume he'll tell me he has no information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He says he doesn't know whether Zejnil Delalic kept his papers there or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm not asking him about any documents particularly in Inda-Bau or not in Inda-Bau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The other papers not in Inda-Bau, how would he know?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of any documents written or signed by Mr. Delalic where the information contained in there about Mr. Delalic's role is blown up or exaggerated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ask him if he has seen any documents first. Only then he can say whether the accounts are blown up or exaggerated.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: He may have information, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ask him whether he has seen those documents. You're asking him specifically about --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Have you ever seen any documents describing Mr. Delalic's role signed or written by Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This question, I don't know. I don't understand. I have no insight into any such documents. I never saw or heard any such things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Have you seen any documents written by Mr. Delalic about his role in the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other documents because you've heard about them or someone described them to you or you just don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of other documents, except these videotapes and newspaper clippings.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, if Mr. Delalic reported in a letter that he was sending a videotape that explained what his role in the war was, do you have any information to indicate what videotape was being referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I never saw such a letter, nor can I say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other videotape that was prepared that describes Mr. Delalic's role in the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly all that was seized from Inda-Bau. I know that those tapes were seized as well as recordings of our folk music that we used to use at our gatherings. So I can't really remember all the details, but these particular tapes that we used, those are the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your testimony, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have no additional questions, Your Honours. But I should like to notify you that we have our next witness, Salih Ruvic, for 2.30. These people arrived late last night after 11.00. I haven't seen the witness. I have to explain how this works, and that is why I have informed the Prosecution that we will be calling him at 2.30 to testify. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are discharged.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will rise and reassemble at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.18 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Will Ms. Residovic proceed with her first witness this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I call witness, Salih Ruvic. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please kindly swear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May it please the court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed. SALIH RUVIC

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please introduce yourself by telling the Trial Chamber your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Salih Ruvic, father's name, Ibro.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Counsel, Mr. Ruvic, before I continue with my questions, as I have done in the case of all previous witnesses, I wish to draw your attention to a technical matter. In view of the fact that both of us speak the same language, it would be very easy for you to answer my questions immediately. However, in the booth up there, interpreters are doing a hard job, so would you please wait until you hear the end of the interpretation on the headphones on the table in front of you and only then begin with the answer to my question. In that way, everyone in the courtroom and their honours, in particular, will be able to follow what the two of us are saying. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do and I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Counsel, thank you. Tell me, please, where and when you were born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on the 17th of August, 1941, in the village of Drunovici, Municipality of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Counsel, what schools have you completed and where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first completed teachers' training school in Sarajevo and then I went on to the university, department for security and defence in Sarajevo and I graduated as an extramural student in May, 1980.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What are you by occupation, Mr. Ruvic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By occupation, I am a teacher of defence and security, but currently I am not working as a teacher, but in the ministry of defence of the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Counsel, Mr. Ruvic, where were you and what were you doing on the 6th of April, 1992, when Bosnia-Herzegovina was declared an independent state and when an aggression was committed against it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 6th of April, 1992, I was performing my duty as commander of the municipal Territorial Defence staff in Prozor, to which post I was appointed by the commander of the district staff in Zenica, Mr. Dzemo Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The municipal staff of Prozor, of which you were the commander, which was the superior command or the superior commander of the municipal staff of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just noted that the municipal staff of Prozor, by order from the staff of the supreme command, was under the command of the district staff of Zenica and the commander of that staff was Dzemo Merdan, as I mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Counsel, until when in 1992 was the municipal staff in Prozor subordinated to the district staff in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The municipal defence staff of Prozor was subordinate to the district staff in Zenica until the beginning of November, 1992, when the 4th corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was formed, headed by now deceased, Mr. Arif Pasalic, with headquarters in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: (Microphone not on).

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately in a traffic accident, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Counsel, Mr. Ruvic, tell me, did you at some point in time in 1992, abandon the post of commander of municipal staff and if you did so, who was appointed commander after you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was commander for less than two months actually and I gave up that position because I didn't agree with a part of the leadership of the SDA party, which was in an alliance with the HVO. The latter would not accept the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina and was following orders exclusively from Grude rather than from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the new commander and can you tell the Trial Chamber who appointed him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander of the municipal staff after me was Mr. Muharem Sabic, who used to be the chief of staff when I was the commander. And he was appointed by the same person as I, that is Mr. Dzemo Merdan from the district staff in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For how long did Mr. Sabic hold the post of commander of the municipal staff of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Sabic remained commander officially, or actually the last day was upon the occupation of Prozor, that is the 25th of October, 1992. When he left, the territory of Prozor municipality and did not return again to that same area. So therefore, until the 25th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Counsel, Mr. Ruvic, after you stopped being commander of the municipal staff, did you remain a member of the municipal staff of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I continued to be a member of the municipal staff and I was assistant commander for operations and training and my task was to regulate the front-line and to assist the commander in establishing the chain of command over TO units in Prozor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Counsel, after Mr. Sabic left his position as commander, did you, at some point in time, again become commander of the Prozor municipal staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Upon the invitation of members of the supreme command, I visited Konjic on the 2nd of November and was provisionally appointed chief of staff. And on the 9th of December of that same day, commander of the municipal staff. I was appointed to this post by Mr. Sefer Halilovic and I received the order by commander of the 4th corps, Mr. Arif Pasalic, who handed it to me. And the document says that the copy is true to the original and it bears the signature of Mr. Arif Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Counsel, in view of all those duties that you performed, Mr. Ruvic, in 1992, in Prozor, I have a number of questions to put to you regarding the responsibilities and jurisdiction over units in Prozor. First, let me ask you, as the commander of the Territorial Defence staff of Prozor at the beginning of the war, can you tell me what kind of weapon the TO staff of Prozor had in its possession?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is it necessary to go into? Let's confine ourselves to what happened in Celebici or what was being commanded as by general's knowledge, commander of TG-1. Let's confine ourselves to that. We're not interested in the weapons. We've already been told that Prozor's weapons were in the Ljuta and they only got 20 per cent of those weapons, when the Ljuta barracks were taken over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that that is an undisputed fact, the witness as one of the regional commanders was able to confirm this fact from the standpoint of his own municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: 50%, 60%, that's really not material for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you know, these witnesses from Jablanica, Prozor and Hadzici have been called only in the context of the responsibility of the command of the tactical group, so that I won't have many questions relating to Celebici itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruvic, please, do you know what Tactical Group 1 is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do know what Tactical Group 1 is. It was a part of the command whose task was in July, 1992, to try and lift the siege of Sarajevo from the direction of Pasaric across Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Counsel, Mr. Ruvic, while you were the commander or a member of the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence of Prozor, were your units reassigned to Tactical Group 1? If they were, please tell us when.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning of June, 1992, we were assigned the task of sending a smaller unit to the front, to seek to lift the siege of Sarajevo. And in mid-June, I personally headed the unit from Prozor, which got as far as Konjic, and from Konjic, together with a unit from Jablanica, and another from Konjic, we went to Pasaric and there we came under the command of Mr. Mustafa Polutak, who was lieutenant colonel at the time and who is now a general of our army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Counsel, Mr. Ruvic, you said a smaller group, can you tell us how many troops that group consisted of, the group you led?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The exact number was 42 soldiers of whom I was the commander for that particular purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Counsel, the other formations of the armed forces of the Territorial Defence of Prozor; under whose command did they remain after you left to carry out this task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They remained under their commander of the municipal staff, Mr. Muharem Sabic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For how long was your unit under the command of Mr. Polutak as the commander of Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think for about six days. I'm not quite sure to the day, but after that we returned to Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Upon your return to Prozor, did those soldiers remain under the command of Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They could not have because they were soldiers belonging to units of the municipal staff, and each one of them returned to their original unit, to the detachment to which they had been assigned originally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruvic, at the time you were the commander and later on, did you know Mr. Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Zejnil Delalic but he didn't know me. This may appear a little strange and illogical. You see, Zejnil's brother lives in Prozor. He got married there; he spent many years there, and he would come for holidays because he spent most of his time abroad working there. I personally met Zejnil Delalic for the first time when I spoke to him in person in mid April 1992 when we asked him to assist us in procuring weapons and equipment for the army, because this was a wealthy person who had a good position. He placed his services at the disposal of the state and the defence of the country, and it was logical that we should look to him for assistance as he had good connections.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruvic, in view of what you have just said, that Mr. Delalic was working for the defence of the country and that he had good business and other connections, how did you at the time in April understand the role of Mr. Zejnil Delalic? Was he civilian and what were the activities he engaged in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I visited Zejnil Delalic together with his brother Zahir known as Zajko, he was a civilian at the time and he engaged in logistic support because, as I said, he was well-to-do and he had the good will and desire to assist the state. We wanted to take advantage of this for him to help us. A moment ago I didn't finish my answer because I wanted to say that we virtually had no weapons. It was stationed in Ljuta in 1990. By orders, all the equipment of the TO was seized and placed in the warehouses of the then JNA in Ljuta.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, learn at some time in '92 that Zejnil Delalic had become a military commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned that Zejnil had been appointed commander of Tactical Group 1 at the beginning of August 1992 and that he succeeded Mr. Mustafa Polutak.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruvic, as you just told us, you were responsible for the combat units in Prozor. Tell me while Mr. Zejnil Delalic was a military commander, were units at that time being reassigned to Zejnil Delalic as the commander of Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a member of the municipal staff, this never happened, nor were we required to do that, but I would have known because I was assistant commander for operations and training.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruvic, could you tell this court whether Zejnil Delalic as commander of Tactical Group 1, did he in any period of time have a superior position over all armed forces in the territory of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This could not have been for two reasons: One was that the HVO did not join in cooperation, nor participate in the TO staff, so that that command could not apply to them. Secondly, the MUP, as a part of the armed forces, also had its own separate chain of command, and he could not have been a superior commander because we belonged to the district staff of Zenica. The commander of that staff was Mr. Dzemo Merdan. Therefore, in view of all this, this was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruvic, did Zejnil Delalic at any point in time act as a superior commander to you personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not, never. He was never my commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, you have answered my question. Now we move to another issue and I will be very brief about this. During that time in 1992 while you were a commander at the beginning of that year, what were the relations between the TO and the HVO in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will have to split my answer in two parts. At the very beginning, the relations were relatively okay until the proclamation of Herceg-Bosna. As soon as Herceg-Bosna was proclaimed, the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, differences became apparent because they no longer recognised any state institutions, and the Territorial Defence of Prozor acted exclusively upon the instructions that we received from the competent republic staff of the Territorial Defence and the then minister of defence, Mr. Jerko Doko.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruvic, could you please tell me whether between the TO and the HVO in Prozor, whether there were any armed conflicts in Prozor or did you hold the line against the enemy together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As of May 1992, the HVO and the army of BiH held the defence line together. It was the line against the Serb Montenegrin aggressor, and the area in question was the territory towards Kupres, the area of Duvno and Gornji Vakuf. We held these positions together. We had our logistics in common, although we had two separate commands and each group had its own commander in the area. Until the 23rd, because the attack on Prozor took place on the 23rd, not the 25th of October, most of the time, over 70 days, I spent on the line near Dolic with my soldiers. As I said, until that time, we used to work together until the critical day when the HVO attacked Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
