utterances.text: Mr. Ruvic, during that period of time, since you were involved with the units of the Territorial Defence in a most immediate, direct way, did you at any point in time receive any order that would have been issued by Mr. Zejnil Delalic as a commander of Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw such an order, and if it had been issued to the commander of the municipal staff, I mean, I would have been the first person who would have been notified of such an order because I was at the line all the time with my soldiers and together with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the witness to be shown Prosecution Exhibit 189. I have a sufficient number of copies here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have indicated that you would have seen any such order had it been issued. Could you now tell us, Mr. Ruvic, if you ever saw this order, if you've ever seen this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This order, the way it is composed and written, I have never seen. I think that Mr. Zejnil Delalic was not in the position to issue such an order simply because he could not order military operations to units who were reassigned, subordinated to a different command. This date here, it is true at that time I was at the position in Dolic, and I would have been advised, I would have known if such an order had been issued, and I would have carried out such an order if it had been issued by my commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruvic, you were present at the front-line at the time. Did you ever withdraw from that line before the attack that took place in October that you mentioned? Did anyone issue orders to that effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not a single unit at that time, not only my unit, ever withdrew from their military assignment until the 22nd of October, that is, the day before the attack on Prozor took place. As I told you, I was at Dolic at the time, and when I learned about the attack on Prozor, when I learned that it would happen, I withdrew with my unit from the positions at Dolic in order to avoid capturing because the order was that we should all be captured.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you a few questions about a different matter, Mr. Ruvic. The commander of the municipal staff, you have already told us who appointed him, was he a member of the war presidency of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Sabic could not be a member of the war presidency, especially in Prozor, because the president of the municipality was a Croat and he was very keen upon directives that he received from Grude that he started receiving at the end of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruvic, you indicated that you were working under the regulations of Bosnia and Herzegovina. According to the regulations of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was it possible for the commander of the municipal staff to be a member of the war presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the decree issued by the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992, commanders of units and staffs were not members of war presidencies. Therefore, Mr. Sabic could not have been a member of the Prozor war presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move to another area. After the attack of the 23rd of October, did members of the staff of the Territorial Defence withdraw from the area of the town of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the aggression, that is, after the 25th of October, all forces of the Territorial Defence withdrew. They withdrew from Prozor on the 24th of October and they were pulled out to the eastern part of the Prozor municipality to the villages of Here, Kute and Scipe. I had already reached the territory of Gornji Vakuf having withdrawn from Dolci. Then from Pridverja (phoen) and Dvorci (phoen), I reported to Mr. Medan in Zenica. I informed him of my positions and I received an order from him to establish a defence line and to go on, to continue with implementing his instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The court already knows about the efforts that were being put forth at that time, but could you tell us whether at that time the population who had been evicted from the area, did they go back to Prozor after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 2nd of 1992, a meeting was held in Prozor --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Ruvic, could you please be brief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'll try to. A meeting was held in Prozor, and from the BiH army, it was Mr. Vehbija Karic who attended the meeting and the Croatian side was represented by Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me whether you took part in any of the groups that were charged with the assessment of the damage that had been done in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just mention one more thing. I was supposed to be there on the said day but I was late for the negotiations in Prozor. However, later on, I took part in the assessment of the damage that was done to the property of Bosniaks in Prozor, and together with a few other members of that group, we assessed the situation. Tens of houses were burned down, including my own, and also a number of houses in the villages of Blace and Memici which is part of the Ogunci (phoen) but the name of the hamlet is Memici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think there's been a mistake in spelling Mr. Vehbija Karic. Anyway, this can be corrected later on. Tell me once again but please try to be brief. Could you tell us whether this attack and everything that occurred at that time was also followed by propaganda against respected people, members of the Bosniak community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence at that time was getting stronger, and when Herceg-Bosna was proclaimed, activities in that regard were being intensified, and there was an intensified campaign against leading persons at the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The information that we received, we kept receiving at that time, were really ridiculous, such as that Mr. Sefer Halilovic had shelled the Croatian area and so on. Mr. Vehbija Karic, who was at the time in Macedonia, or some other politicians were also attacked. This was supposed to sew hatred between our two communities and this was supposed to confuse our community, the community of Bosniaks so that it would be easier for other forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina to act against us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruvic, were you personally object of such campaign?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not only myself, but a certain number of other prominent citizens in Prozor who were at the time the target of such a campaign. I will give you an example. When I was in the fourth corps, I was shown a document from the HVO whereby it was stated that I was a KOS officer, officer from a former intelligence service, and that I also underwent some kind of training and that I had been in Nis a long time ago, but I had only passed through Nis a couple of times a long time ago while I was serving in the JNA before the war and that was it. I had never been in Nis before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ruvic, do you know where the Celebici barracks is located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know where the Celebici barracks is located because it's not far from here. It's in the village called Celebici in the direction of Jablanica and I know that that used to be barracks even before the war. Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruvic, did you at any point in time in 1992 visit this barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no need to go to the Celebici barracks, and I never went there. My work didn't require such a trip.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there ever a time in 1992 that you heard or learned that the barracks in Celebici had been the site of some mistreatment against detainees? Did you ever hear that prisoners in the area of Konjic had been mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992, no, I didn't hear anything about that. As I told you, I spent most of the time at the front-line. Yes, maybe later on I did hear something, but that was after that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruvic, since you were staff commander in Prozor, after all these attempts to resolve the situation, did the situation calm down at any point in time in 1992? I'm referring to the relations between you and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Attempts were made at the beginning of November 1992 to resolve the situation but to no avail, although a number of people returned to Prozor on the basis of a joint declaration which was written at that meeting. On the 13th of January, 1993 when the HVO and the HVO carried out an attack against Donji Vakuf, the village of Here also came under attack as well as the rest of the municipality of Prozor which had not been under the HVO control until that time, so the situation was not settled. Jablanica was also attacked later on. However, upon an initiative of the European community headed by Mr. Rajmon Glenn (phoen), a series of three or four meetings took place in Prozor at the end of March, beginning of April. I think the first one took place on the 17th of March in Prozor and we tried to find an agreement. However, because of the attacks on Jablanica and later on on Konjic, there could be no talk about any kind of agreement. Former members of the Territorial Defence were subsequently arrested. Over 900 military aged men were arrested and taken to concentration camps in the areas of Prozor, Grude, Capljina, Heliodrom and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, this concludes my examination of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination of him?

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ruvic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: My name is Nico Duric and I represent here Mr. Zdravko Mucic. Do you know Mr. Zdravko Mucic by any chance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know Mr. Zdravko Mucic. The first time I heard his name was when his arrest was made public in the papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: You have indicated sometime ago that during 1992, the HVO, that is, the relations between the HVO and the Territorial Defence, that is, the forces of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were relatively good only to be exacerbated later on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I was referring to the initial period until the formation of Herceg-Bosna because Croats had voted for Bosnia and Herzegovina before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruvic. Can you tell us now, do you know the village of Ravno? Have you ever heard of that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Wait a minute. There is a village called Ravno in the municipality of Kupres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: But do you know a village called Ravno much further down in the area of Dubrovnik also in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have heard about that village, but I have never been there and I couldn't tell you exactly where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Whose village is it? Do you know if it's a Croatian village, a Serb village or a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether I know the structure of the population, but I believe that it was a Croat village by majority. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ruvic, do you know what happened with that village at the end of 1991, beginning of '92?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that a number of bad things happened in that area. I don't know exactly what. I didn't have access to information. I believe that a massacre took place and that people were evicted from that village. I couldn't be more specific. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: You said "bad things." It seems that you know more about what happened there. Could you be more precise, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He's telling you he couldn't be specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How are we interested in that village?

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as regards to the relationship between the HVO and the TO that my learned colleague Edina Residovic was questioning him about, because of the reasons why these -- why there was this worsening of the relationships between the HVO and the TO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But there was evidence that there was a worsening of the relationship. They didn't take part after having agreed in that campaign against the Borci area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: I'm going at the very outset what sparked the whole conflict, but it does have a bearing on the whole case. I would say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask a few questions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: About what he hasn't known properly?

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Because it appears that the whole thing just happened out of the blue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If he has indicated ignorance in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Don't try to defend Croats or Bosniaks because you're not here for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not defending them. No, I'm not doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We're just not interested in that dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Okay. That concludes my examination. Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. Ruvic. I have no more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Don't raise questions here with which we're not concerned. We're concerned with the Celebici camp. If these questions have any bearing on what happened inside Celebici, please do ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: The Defence of Hazim Delic has no questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McMurrey?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence of Esad Landzo has no questions for this witness either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Does the Prosecution have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution does have questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Ruvic, you were shown Exhibit 189 which, I think, is the document that is still in front of you there; do you see that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said that you would have obeyed this order had you received it, but you don't ever recall receiving it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is not what the witness said, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I had received an order from my commander of the municipal staff, I would have respected it from my TO commander. If I had received it from my commander, I would have obeyed it, but such an order never reached me because I was there on those lines and I stayed there and therefore this had no bearing whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had you obeyed this order if you received this one, particularly Exhibit 189?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He qualified it from his commander. If he would have received it from his commander, he would have obeyed it. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If my municipal staff commander had received this order from the commander of the district staff for Zenica, as an obedient member of the staff, I would have carried out the order of my superior commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question is: If you had received this particular order signed by Zejnil Delalic, would you have obeyed this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not have obeyed it because Zejnil Delalic was not a superior to military structures of the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Prozor, but rather it was Mr. Dzemo Merdan from the Zenica district staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How would you know whether or not this was an order issued directly by him or one that was merely passed on by him from the supreme command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Commanders act on the basis of written orders and on the basis of instructions and orders from their superiors. So when somebody issues an order, he has to sign it and stamp it. In this case, there's no stamp of the Zenica district staff and such an order would not have been obeyed even if Sabic had received it. If he had received it, he would have had to inform Mr. Dzemo Merdan in the Zenica district staff to ask him for further instructions, and this was not done because the army did not withdraw and it stayed on at the joint defence lines towards Kupres and Ravno, but not the Ravno counsel was referring to but the Ravno in Kupres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that there was no incident between Croats and Muslims on that date or round about that date, the 27th and 28th of August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me see. On that day, the 27th, the 28th -- the 27th, I went to Idovac and I was about 30 kilometres from Prozor, the slopes of Mount Idovac. And afterwards I learned that a small group of members of HVO were in Prozor. They attempted to demolish some shops, but the Commander Sabic issued orders that not a single member of the TO may do anything so as not to ignite a conflict, and a conflict did not break out. This group did break in, but the very next day the Croats condemned this damage and expressed readiness to compensate for it, but this had no influence on the cooperation and further activities between the army and the HVO in Prozor at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On the 27th and 28th of August, 1992, members of the HVO and HOS attacked buildings and facilities owned by prominent and well-off Muslims in Prozor, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just told you. That evening, I learned this subsequently because I was in the field, but a group of irresponsible persons, and there are such persons everywhere and in any army and especially so in this war, who tried to deal out justice, but they failed because they were prevented by their own superiors, but this did not upset -- this minor incident did not upset relations between the Bosniaks and the Croats in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It's not quite the way you're telling it, is it? As a matter of fact, one of the criticisms were that the Croatian officials in the HVO had difficulty restraining their extremists, didn't they? That was one of the complaints.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid you didn't understand me well. I said that within the HVO and among the HOS who came from outside, there were individuals who didn't want us to have good relations and to defend the lines jointly. I said that they were denounced by their own people. During the war, any one who was in Bosnia would be able to see for himself that there were individuals who wanted to settle personal accounts and they were out of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now very early in the piece, you resigned as commander of the Territorial Defence because of the fact that the HVO wouldn't take orders from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning I said -- if necessary, I can repeat that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You don't have to repeat it in detail, just say "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it once again for me to understand what you're asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am saying very early in the piece, soon after you're appointed as commander of the Territorial Defence, you resigned from that position because of the fact that the HVO declined to take its orders from Sarajevo and took its orders from Grude; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right. I said that with the formation of Herceg-Bosna and when orders came from the state presidency to form municipal staffs which had ceased operating in some municipalities, including Prozor, and the deadline for forming staffs was April the 15th, and that was the last day for the registration of municipal staffs. That day is taken as the day of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Croats did not wish to join that new staff, and commanders to the HVO were brought from the outside, three of them, until the fall of Prozor came from outside the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were not even citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. After that, even Praljak, who was in Prozor during the HVO attack on Prozor, even he is not a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but is an officer of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Indeed, I think that part of your complaint was that they were not only taken orders from Grude, but from Zagreb as well? A "yes" or "no" answer will suffice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were receiving instructions from Zagreb because they tried to establish their authority. They said Prozor had to belong the Banovina, the Split county. In the autumn of '92/'93, they tried to introduce curricular based on Croatian programs which the teachers, Bosniaks, would not agree to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I do not see the relevance of these questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the SDA party which you argued with and which brought about your resignation, was that the local branch or was that the SDA in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the local branch, the local branch. I said a part of the party leadership, not all of them, a part of the leadership. If necessary, I can give you the name of the man in question, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, it's not necessary. Please tell me who were the members of the Prozor municipal staff, the main members of it? There's yourself and who else? Can you tell me their positions or titles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me see, the first commander at the beginning, there was me, my deputy was Mr. Hero Mustafa and chief of staff, Mr. Muharem Sabic. In addition to them, there were several others. I don't know whether you need all the names of all the members. If necessary, I can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, no, I am mainly interested in organisations. Was the MUP represented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The MUP is a part of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It has its own command, its own chain of command. But in combat operations, MUP units are a regular component part of the defence forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but they have their own control and command through the republican MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They have their own chain of command, but their actions are coordinated in the field, aren't they, between the MUP and the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, the MUP is a component part of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, one of the parts. It has its own chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's not part of the TO. It's not a part of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's not a part --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, they are part of the armed forces. They are not part of the TO. Because at the beginning in '92, the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina were comprised of the Territorial Defence, the HVO and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, can you answer this question for me: When you're conducting a military operation into the field, does the MUP go off and do its own thing and the TO does its own thing or is there some sort of coordinated action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you, it depends on the order. Whoever is in command of a particular operation orders the use of units, the deployment of units and who will be in command of those units at that point in time. This is not such a strict rule. You see, when an operation in prepared and planned, there is an order as to who will be in command, which are the component units and formations, and who will be in command of them. The assignments are determined by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And is the MUP in command of the TO or is the TO in command of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The MUP was never in command of TO units, but very often in Bosnia-Herzegovina, members of MUP did participate in combat operations as members of the armed forces. As by law, they are a component part of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Under certain circumstances, they would come under the command of the municipal TO, wouldn't they, when that was happening, when they were out in joint action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In concrete terms, in the area of Prozor, MUP never participated in the armed forces or the armed operations until the end -- no, until 1995 by when there was the 4th corps, and MUP representatives were given certain tasks by their own commanders and they carried out those tasks in particular areas, front-line operations and so on. But in Prozor, such joint activities by the MUP and the Territorial Defence never took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you were participating in military activities in the year of 1992 in the Prozor region, did you at any stage ever take prisoners of war or arrest anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I personally was a commander of the municipal staff, we didn't have any prisoners of war. But afterwards in 1993, there were three prisoners, all of them were returned or, rather, exchanged. While I was in command because I was commander of the municipal staff, and then by orders of co-commanders, the commanders of units were appointed and they carried out their combat assignment. So that I did not participate in the commanding of these units after February 1993. When by instruction from Mr. Arif Pasalic, an officer from the 4th Corps, was appointed battalion commander, Vujanovic known as Haja.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is it right to say that during the whole period of 1992 the Territorial Defence of Prozor didn't take one prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct. Throughout 1992, the Territorial Defence of Prozor had no prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, in the early stages of the war in the early part in April of 1992, were there any volunteer groups or volunteers or Green Berets, people that call themselves Green Berets or volunteers that you know of that were operating in the Prozor area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the formation of the TO staff on April the 1st, 1992, of which I was the commander, all the units that had been self-organised in individual villages placed themselves under the command of the municipal Territorial Defence staff. Outside that staff, after April the 1st, 1992, there were no other units as far as the members Bosniaks are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I am referring to. The Green Berets were only operational up until the 1st of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, until then, because then I toured the whole municipality in person, and in some villages like the villages of Here, Kute, Scipe, Donji Kraj, Grevici and some other villages southwards towards Jablanica, they were people who had self-organised themselves because people realised the danger because the aggression had already started on Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 6th of April. All units were placed under the control of the Territorial Defence staff 100 per cent. This is 100 per cent true. Everything else is false and there is ample evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I wasn't suggesting anything was false, but anyway, we'll move on. Now, you said that you saw Mr. Delalic prior to him becoming TG-1 commander and that he didn't perform a military function. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had met Mr. Delalic before August twice, the first time in mid-April, 1992, when we sought assistance from him to help us in obtaining weapons and equipment, which we were short of. And the second time I met him was when we went to Hadzici to try to deblock Sarajevo. And then, I don't know in what capacity Mr. Delalic addressed us in front of the motel in Konjic and wished us a safe journey and success in our endeavour to deblock Sarajevo because Sarajevo was a symbol of the state and it was an honour for me. I considered it to be a privilege to participate in such operations, that is to deblock Sarajevo and Mr. Zejnil assisted us logistically at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now when you saw Mr. Delalic on either occasion, was he wearing a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time he wasn't, I am 100%. And the second time I am not quite sure because this was six years ago. But I know that he didn't have any military function, any function, which doesn't mean to say that he may not have had any duties --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The second occasion he was wearing a uniform, that's the end. On the 1st, he was definitely not wearing and on the second you're not sure. That is the end of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You'd agree with me, wouldn't you, that had you have met Mr. Delalic and he had a military uniform on and he was wearing his insignia of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then you'd have a totally different opinion, wouldn't you, about whether he had a military function?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: (Microphone not on).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But I am asking whether he would because he is a soldier surely he can answer that question, Your Honour. Well, we'll find out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was saying that I cannot say with certainty whether he had a uniform on him or not, but I do not know for certain that he addressed us, that he wished us all the best and that he had helped us in obtaining equipment and armaments and he gave us some clothing and some Motorola’s, which we used as communications equipment. And he did so through his brother who was living in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now his brother is Zahir Delalic, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zahir Delalic, known Zajka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what role did he play in Prozor during the period of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the formation of the TO staff of Territorial Defence, Mr. Zahir Delalic was a member of the leadership of the SDA party and he placed himself in the service of the country's defence. And when I abandoned my position, he assisted us logistically and he was a member -- he was not immediately a member of the municipal staff, but after I left, Mr. Sabic appointed him as advisor, as his advisor for certain areas in the municipal staff of Prozor municipality. And there must be a written document about that. Because on one occasion I actually saw that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, you said in your evidence that the deterioration of relationships between the Croatian community, the HDZ and the BiH didn't really happen until late, as late as October of 1992, and I think I am correctly stating the evidence. But, I show you this document now and I ask you to look at it. I have a copy for Your Honours and for the defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It relates to Prozor?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It does indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Document 247.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid that you didn't understand me very well at first. I said that with the formation of the TO staff of Prozor, the Croats would not participate in the joint command, in the joint municipality staff of Territorial Defence, even though they had promised to do so. Because in the night of the 14th to the 15th of April, we sent in our registration. However, the next few days, a joint municipal staff, which was to have numbered fifteen; six Bosniaks and nine Croats, was not formed because they did not agree because they started receiving instructions from Grude, which is an outpost of Zagreb and they did not agree. They told us openly at a meeting, which they convened, they told us, there can be no TO in Prozor. It will be either the HVO or the Chetniks, so it's up to you gentlemen, Bosniaks. And at that meeting held in the parts supply institution, I said that it was a privilege to defend the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I said, damn every Bosniak that doesn't defend Bosnia-Herzegovina, it's our only state, the only country we have. And that we accept anyone who is in favour of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina; anyone who is against it is our enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How many soldiers from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's interesting SDS a critical part --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, the interpreters cannot interpret for the witness. Microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's an interesting document. It refers to a crisis staff of a political party, SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I don't know the explanation of that, Your Honour. But it seems to be that the SDS was representing, from what I can see, the present municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's an SDA document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Not to the municipality or the municipal staff. It's interesting from this point of view, that the political party also formed crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How many soldiers were there from the Prozor Territorial Defence allocated to Tactical Group 1? Can you remember? If you can't remember it doesn't matter, because you may not have that information at hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has answered this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that there were 42 with me, 42 soldiers of whose commander I was. I was in command of those soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry if you answered that part, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now I take it you didn't see every order sent to the command of the Prozor Territorial Defence during the time that you were there, or did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said at first that I saw all the orders, but when I ceased being commander, it was the duty of the commander to brief me about things that concerned me, or which would have helped us to make the right decision, of course, under those circumstances. And all the other decisions that had nothing to do with me and in which I didn't have to participate, it was not my duty to know everything because the commanders may have information which other members of the staff need not have. That is his discretion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: -- from the Territorial Defence participate in JUG '92?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you're asking me this for the third time. I said that in 1992, members of the Territorial Defence from Prozor, participated in the attempt to lift the blockade of Sarajevo in Hadzici. When we got there, this unit was placed under the command of Mr. Mustafa Polutak. A couple of days later, he'd returned, each member went back to his former unit and no combat operations until the HVO attack on Prozor until the 28th of October, '92. There were no other attacks until then in which members of the Territorial Defence of Prozor municipality participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I think you said that Mr. Zahir Delalic was advisor to the Prozor territorial command. Do you know why he went to Celebici from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I know he was an advisor to the commander. The commander would give him assignments to go to Konjic because he is originally from Konjic. Their family was living there. Why he went to see his brother, that is something Commander Sabic should know. I didn't know what his assignments, what his tasks were when he went to Konjic because I didn't need to know that. Anyway, I told you that I spent most of my time in the field with the army on the front lines near Kupres facing the Serb Montenegro aggressor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we'll have to call a break, except you're winding up. If you're not, we'll break and come back after.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not winding up, Your Honour, I have one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said that you heard information or you received information about Celebici, not in 1992, but later. My question is what information did you receive? What did you hear about Celebici later? What was it that you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific in putting your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You're asked a question, whether you'd heard about things that had happened at Celebici and you said you didn't hear anything in the year of 1992, but you heard things later. My question is what it was that you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This later meant much later. I heard that according to the accusations against the gentleman, there was some kind of concentration camp in Celebici, which it couldn't have been. But what happened there as this is far away, Prozor is 54 kilometres from Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay, that's all I wanted the know, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any re-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. No re-examination for this witness. This is the last witness the defence has for this hearing, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You no longer have any witnesses that you are calling for today?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Not for today, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We are not sitting on Monday here, there's an United Nations holiday. I think you now see the trend. If you haven't made arrangements to call witnesses for next week to cover, you better take this opportunity to supplement the list of witnesses, so that we should increase them by at least you double the number of witnesses. We are taking at least a minimum of two a day. So that will be able to cover the period between Tuesday and Friday. That should be the pattern all along from next week. I think since we have nothing more...

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will analyse the testimony of the witnesses we have heard so far and on Tuesday morning, we will give you a final list. According to our estimate, we will continue reducing the number of witnesses in line with your suggestions, Your Honour. Thank you. For this week, I think we did our best and I think we heard seven witnesses in a week, which I think is the first time since we have been at trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: My projection is that it could be even more. You could have up to ten if you really follow the evidence that they are coming to give. If you really follow strictly, you don't have to take a long time for each witness. Because all of these witnesses don't have more than their own jurisdiction to testify to. So when you expand it and include areas which you will get to them, other than areas for which they should legitimately testify to, then we have the problems. It's not only you, also the Prosecution. There are places where you speculate, a person ought to have knowledge, when, in fact, ideally, he does not have the knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There's one thing I would like to bring to your notice here. We had that document whereby your client was made commander of all formations. That document has been slightly differently translated in the documents filed by brigadier, those three volumes. I don't know which translation is correct. Please check up on that. Because yours is all formations and the translation given to us from those documents produced by the brigadier, it says, "All units in the line". That would make a different document all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We'll have a look into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, we'll check. Thank you very much for drawing our attention to this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Trial Chamber will now adjourn until Tuesday at ten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 2nd day of June, 1998 at 10.00 a.m. 25
